question: How far can the danger zone extend from the front bumper of a school bus, and which part of that zone is most dangerous?
choice_a: Up to 30 feet from the front bumper, with the first 10 feet being the most dangerous
choice_b: 10 feet total, with the last 5 feet being most dangerous
choice_d: The danger zone only exists behind the bus
explanation: Danger zones extend as much as 30 feet from the front bumper (the first 10 feet being most dangerous), 10 feet from each side, and 10 feet behind the rear bumper.

question: When properly adjusted, how far behind the bus should the outside left and right side flat mirrors let a driver see?
choice_b: 200 feet or 4 bus lengths behind the bus
choice_d: There is no distance standard for flat mirrors
explanation: Flat mirrors should be adjusted to show 200 feet or 4 bus lengths behind the bus, along the sides, and the rear tires touching the ground.
source_note: Section 10.1.3 - Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: When approaching a school bus stop where students will be loaded, when should the driver activate alternating flashing amber warning lights?
choice_a: Only after the bus has come to a complete stop
choice_c: At least 200 feet, or about 5-10 seconds, before the school bus stop
choice_d: Amber lights are never required, only red lights
explanation: If equipped, activate alternating flashing amber warning lights at least 200 feet, or approximately 5-10 seconds, before the school bus stop (or per state law).

question: When stopping to load students, how far away from the students should the front bumper of the bus come to a stop?
choice_a: Right next to the students so they don't have to walk
choice_b: Distance does not matter as long as the flashers are on
choice_d: At least 10 feet away, forcing students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements
explanation: Bring the bus to a full stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet from students, which forces them to walk to the bus, giving the driver a better view of their movements.

question: After unloading students along the route, how far should students walk away from the side of the bus before the driver pulls away?
choice_a: At least 10 feet away from the side of the bus, to a position where the driver can plainly see them
choice_b: They should stay right next to the bus
explanation: Students should exit and walk at least 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a position where the driver can plainly see all of them before the bus pulls away.
source_note: Section 10.2.3 - Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: If a student is missed at an unloading stop along the route, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Immediately back up to the stop
choice_b: Not back up; instead follow local procedures
choice_c: Call the student's parents before continuing
choice_d: Continue the route and report it at the end of the day only
explanation: If you have missed a student's unloading stop, do not back up -- be sure to follow local procedures instead.
source_note: Section 10.2.3 - Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: Why should a driver walk through the bus after unloading students at school?
choice_a: It is not necessary if the bus looks empty from the driver's seat
choice_b: Only to check the fuel gauge
choice_c: To check for hiding or sleeping students and items left behind
explanation: The driver should walk through the bus to check for hiding or sleeping students and any items left by students before leaving the unloading area.

question: Under which of the following conditions MUST a driver evacuate a school bus?
choice_b: Whenever the bus is running more than 10 minutes late
choice_c: Only when directed by dispatch, never on the driver's own judgment
choice_d: The bus is on fire (or threatened by fire), stalled on or adjacent to a railroad crossing, or there is imminent danger of collision
explanation: Mandatory evacuation situations include the bus being on fire or threatened by fire, stalled on or adjacent to a railroad crossing, in a position where danger may increase, in imminent danger of collision, or facing a hazardous materials spill requiring quick evacuation.

question: During an evacuation, how far off the road (in the direction of oncoming traffic) should a 'safe place' generally be?
choice_a: At least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic
explanation: A safe place should be at least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic, to keep students from being hit by debris if another vehicle collides with the bus.

question: At a railroad crossing with gates, what should a driver do if the gate stays down after the train has passed?
choice_b: Not drive around the gate; instead call the dispatcher
choice_c: Break through the gate since it is designed to give way
choice_d: Wait exactly 5 minutes, then proceed regardless
explanation: If the gate stays down after the train passes, do not drive around it -- call your dispatcher instead.

question: At a railroad-highway crossing, how close should a school bus stop to the nearest rail?
choice_a: No closer than 5 feet and no farther than 25 feet
choice_c: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet
choice_d: There is no set range, any safe distance is fine
explanation: Stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail, at the point with the best view of the tracks.

question: If a school bus stalls or becomes trapped on railroad tracks, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Try to restart the engine repeatedly before evacuating
choice_b: Move students to the rear of the bus for protection
choice_c: Wait inside the bus for the train to stop
choice_d: Get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving away from the tracks and toward the train
explanation: If the bus stalls or is trapped on the tracks, get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving at an angle away from the tracks and toward the train.
source_note: Section 10.4.4 - Bus Stalls or Trapped on Tracks

question: In an emergency stop, how should a driver brake a school bus equipped with ABS?
choice_a: Use only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control, without pumping the brakes
choice_b: Pump the brakes rapidly, just as with a non-ABS vehicle
choice_c: Release the brakes completely and steer only
choice_d: ABS requires a completely different braking technique from normal driving
explanation: Brake as you always have, using only the force necessary to stop safely and stay in control; in emergency braking, do not pump the brakes on a bus equipped with ABS.

question: Is backing a school bus generally recommended, and what is required if there is no choice but to back up?
choice_a: Backing is encouraged as the safest way to reposition; no special procedure is needed
choice_b: Backing is strongly discouraged; if unavoidable, use a lookout, signal for quiet, and back slowly and smoothly, never with students outside the bus
choice_c: Backing is only allowed at highway speeds
choice_d: A lookout is optional as long as mirrors are checked
explanation: Backing a school bus is strongly discouraged and should only be done when there's no other safe option; the driver should post a lookout, signal for quiet, and back slowly and smoothly, never while students are outside the bus.

question: What is 'tail swing' on a school bus, and roughly how far can it extend?
choice_a: The sway of the bus at highway speed; up to 1 foot
choice_b: A term for excessive brake fade; not measured in feet
choice_c: The outward movement of the rear of the bus during a turn; up to three feet
choice_d: The distance the bus rolls back on a hill; up to 6 feet
explanation: A school bus can have up to a three-foot tail swing -- the outward movement of the rear of the bus during a turn -- so drivers must check mirrors before and during turns.
